title: Microbench regression hypothesis: INT8 vs FP8 signal-noise
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note to capture a narrow microbenchmark-driven hypothesis for a regression we've observed across a small but high-signal set of customer traces. The regression appears when switching some models from FP8 kernels to INT8 kernels under light concurrency (1-4 concurrent requests) and short sequence lengths (<64). This doc lays out the hypothesis, quick experiments to reproduce, initial data, suspected root causes, and next steps for instrumentation and mitigation.

Context / Why this matters:
- Several hosted customers reported subtle output differences after automatic routing started preferring INT8 variants for cost reasons. Differences are small but frequent on short prompts (e.g., system messages, short Q/A).
- Unit economics push us to use INT8 aggressively, but we must avoid quality regressions for short-tail, high-frequency requests (chat startup tokens, routing metadata).
- Existing large-scale quantization dashboards aggregate over long sequences and high concurrency; they miss micro-patterns where kernel scheduling and batching decisions change micro-latency and KV cache timings, which can affect determinism and final tokens.

Observed signals (raw notes):
- customer reported: "answers sound more generic; token choices differ at start" (multiple reports, low severity individually)
- internal A/B on short prompt set (n=2k prompts) showed ~2.4% token-level divergence between FP8 baseline and INT8 variant for first 16 tokens; divergence decays by token 40.
- p50 latency improved ~8% with INT8; p99 unchanged.
- per-request profiler traces show different kernel invocation ordering and variable k-v cache warmup timing.
- retracing runs with same random seed produced non-identical outputs when using INT8 kernels but were deterministic on FP8.

Hypothesis (short):
Small-sequence, low-concurrency requests amplify scheduling nondeterminism and quantization noise in INT8 kernels because:
1) INT8 kernels enable more aggressive micro-batching and different op-fusion paths; this changes the exact timing of KV-cache insertions and read-backs for early tokens. Some kernels/paths are implemented with slightly different rounding/accumulation ordering leading to bit-level differences that then amplify in autoregressive decoding for the first few tokens.
2) FP8 execution path uses a fused kernel that preserves accumulation order (and possibly uses different scaling heuristics), yielding more stable early-token outputs.
3) Low concurrency reduces masking of timing differences that would average out in heavy batching regimes.

Threat model / when this is user-visible:
- Short prompts: system instructions, name/value completions, one-shot Q/A where a single token divergence at token 3-8 changes punctuation or a function call trigger.
- Deterministic workflows that rely on exact-token equality between runs (rare but exists in some integration tests).

Quick reproduction plan (commands / data):
1) Use our microbench harness: tools/microbench/runner --model rwd-open-13b --variant int8-kernel-X --prompt-set prompts/short-system-2k.json --seed 42 --batch-size 1 --concurrency 1 --max-tokens 64 --record-traces=on --out=artifact_int8.json
2) Same run with variant fp8-kernel-Y --> artifact_fp8.json
3) Script to compute token-level divergence and first-token-change-rate: tools/analysis/compare_tokens.py artifact_fp8.json artifact_int8.json --metrics first_token_flip_rate,token_divergence@k=16 > diff_short_2k.tsv
4) Capture GPU perf counters during runs: nvprof/perf with counters: l2_cache_hit_rate,sm_efficiency,warp_serialize,dram_utilization. Note any smear in execution time across kernels.

Initial results (first pass):
- first_token_flip_rate = 3.2% (int8 vs fp8) on short-system-2k.json
- token_divergence@16 = 2.1%
- retrace runs (repeat same command) with int8 variant had non-zero Hamming across runs in ~0.4% of requests (suspected nondeterminism in kernel path), fp8 retraces were stable at 0.0%.
- nvprof: int8 path showed higher warp_serialize on certain fused kernels; FP8 path showed slightly higher shared mem reuse.
- Perf shows an extra kernel call per block in int8 path for small sequence windows (kernel overhead isn't amortized).

Suspected root causes (detailed):
- Kernel numeric ordering: INT8 path uses per-block accumulation with 32-bit accumulation and a final requantize op that can reorder sums compared to FP8 fused matmul+accum. Even with same seed, floating-rounding can differ.
- Scheduler micro-batch grouping heuristics: for batch=1, sequence<64, an INT8 codepath triggers an opportunistic kernel that attempts mini-batching across tokens/reuse; the implementation uses atomic updates to a shared buffer when concurrency>0 but falls back to single-threaded path when concurrency=1 — subtle code difference exists.
- Uninitialized padding lanes: some INT8 kernels rely on zeroing unused lanes differently than FP8 fused kernels; tiny garbage data in padding may leak into accumulation if a code path misses an explicit memset under rare memory alignment.
- Nonzero nondeterminism windows: a race condition in a custom kernel used for int8-remap for certain layer shapes that is masked by FP8 fused kernel implementation.

Immediate mitigations to try (low-risk):
- Add an INT8 deterministic flag that forces a slower-but-deterministic kernel variant for batch-size 1 and seq<128. (short-term: avoids regression for low-concurrency chats)
- Adjust automatic routing to prefer FP8 for routes with median prompt length < 48 for first 2k requests to reduce user surface area while we debug.
- Add a quick memory-zero patch on the INT8 padding code to rule out stray data contribution.

Instrumentation changes needed:
- Add token-level stochastic divergence metric to the per-route dashboard (first-token-flip-rate, cumulative divergence at k). Currently we only show overall perplexity/regressions aggregated across long sequences.
- Add mandatory retrace-on-regression flag: when float-equivalent divergence > 0.5% on short prompts, rerun 3 times and surface nondeterminism rate in alert.
- Add kernel-level trace tagging in profiler output so we can map token divergence to specific kernel IDs and kernel args in the trace. We need to propagate call-site file/line into runtime traces.

Next experiments (priority order):
1) Narrow down to layer(s): run layer-swap tests where early layers execute in FP8 while later layers use INT8 to see where divergence originates.
2) Microstep: instrument logits after each layer for a small sample and compare L2 difference between FP8 and INT8 per layer across tokens 1-16.
3) Determinism stress test: run 10k single-shot runs for each variant with identical seeds and measure nondeterminism rate; capture kernel trace when nondeterminism observed.
4) Alignment test: vary memory alignments and zeroing to see if padding garbage contributes.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- Is the nondeterminism coming from an actual race in the INT8 kernel, or from nondeterministic scheduling that changes numerical accumulation order?
- Does FP8 numerics inherently stabilize early tokens because of fused/op-ordered accumulation?
- Are there model-architecture shapes (hidden size multiples, attention head counts) that are more sensitive? (action: run on 7B, 13B, 70B small-shape variants)
- Does enabling strict deterministic math (CUDA deterministic flags) eliminate differences? (if yes, then scheduling).

Quick TODOs (owners):
- Maya: run layer-swap microbench (2k prompts) and capture layer-wise logits (due 2026-08-14)
- Evan: add kernel-id tagging to profiler trace (PR draft) and run deterministic stress test (due 2026-08-16)
- Diego: prototype INT8 deterministic fallback kernel flag and test overhead (due 2026-08-18)
- Laura: update per-route dashboard spec for first-token metrics and link to alerting (due 2026-08-20)

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- This feels like a hybrid of numeric sensitivity + micro-scheduling. The customer impact is small today but could be amplified by more aggressive INT8 routing.
- Keep an eye on model evals where early-token semantics drive function-calling triggers (these are high-risk).
- If we find a nondeterministic kernel, escalate to SRE for a repro with hardware counters and exact driver/runtime versions.

References / related artifacts:
- quick A/B results: gs://redwood-results/microbench/short-system-2k/ab_summary.csv
- earlier stability notes (related): CONFLUENCE-5310 (quant-stability-overview)
- pending PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4721 (kernel-id tagging)

End of note.

(Leave comments inline — rough doc, will convert to a formal postmortem / investigation page once we have deterministic repro.)
